metals-alloys-s2.title: Pure copper and two copper alloys
metals-alloys-s2.text: A student tests three annealed (heat-softened) wires of the same thickness. Hardness is on a scale where a larger number means harder to dent. The metallic radius of each element is given.

table.caption: Composition, atomic radii and test results

items.q: Which box represents an interstitial alloy?
options: Box W
Box X
Box Y
Box W and Box Y

why.correct: In an interstitial alloy, much smaller atoms (here carbon) fit into the gaps between the larger metal atoms, which stay in their usual places. Box X shows that: steel.
options: Box W is pure iron: one kind of atom only.
Right: small atoms in the holes of the iron lattice.
In Box Y the second element's atoms take the places of iron atoms; that is a substitutional alloy.
Box W is a pure metal and Box Y is substitutional; neither has atoms in the gaps.

items.q: Which element is most likely the second metal in Box Y? (Radii: Fe 126 pm, Cr 128 pm, Ca 197 pm, K 227 pm, B 84 pm)
options: Calcium, Ca
Potassium, K
Boron, B
Chromium, Cr

why.correct: A substitutional alloy forms when the added atoms are about the same size as the host atoms, so they can take their places in the lattice. Cr (128 pm) is almost the same size as Fe (126 pm); stainless steel contains chromium this way.
options: Ca (197 pm) is far larger than Fe, so it does not fit in an iron atom's place.
K (227 pm) is far too large to replace Fe in its lattice.
B (84 pm) is much smaller than Fe; small atoms fit between the iron atoms instead, as in Box X.
Right: nearly the same radius as Fe.

items.q: The material in Box X is harder and less malleable than the material in Box W. Which explanation is best?
options: Carbon atoms in the gaps block the iron layers from sliding past each other
The carbon atoms take electrons from the sea, so fewer electrons hold iron together
The carbon atoms make the iron atoms larger, so the iron atoms pack more tightly
Carbon is a nonmetal, so its atoms form ionic bonds with the iron atoms

why.correct: A metal bends because its layers of atoms can slide past one another, with the electron sea holding them together throughout. Small atoms wedged between the layers act like pins: the layers catch on them and resist sliding. The metal becomes harder, stronger and less malleable.
options: Right: the interstitial atoms block the layers from sliding.
The harder alloy is still held by metallic bonding; the change comes from the atoms blocking movement, not from fewer electrons.
The carbon atoms do not change the size of the iron atoms.
The carbon atoms sit in a metallic lattice; steel is not an ionic compound.

items.q: Which statements are true of all three samples in boxes W, X and Y? Select all that apply.
options: They conduct electricity because they contain delocalized electrons.
Their atoms are held together by metallic bonding.
They are made of a single element.
They contain atoms of two different sizes in the gaps between atoms.

why.correct: Pure iron and both alloys are metallic solids: cations in a sea of delocalized electrons, so all three conduct and all are held by metallic bonding.
options: Right: the electron sea is present in all three.
Right: alloys keep the metallic bonding of their main metal.
Only Box W is a single element; X and Y are alloys, mixtures of elements.
Only Box X has atoms in the gaps; in Y the second element replaces iron atoms.

items.q: In Box Y, what percent of the atoms are atoms of the second metal?

mistakes.why: Value: you divided by the number of iron atoms (15). Divide by the total number of atoms (20).

why.correct: Box Y has 20 atoms, 5 of them the second metal: 5 ÷ 20 × 100 = 25%.

items.q: Which kind of alloy are brass and bronze, based on the atomic radii?
options: Interstitial: the added atoms are larger than Cu atoms
Interstitial: the added atoms fit into the gaps between Cu atoms
Substitutional: the added atoms are close in size to Cu
Neither: an alloy needs a nonmetal to be added

why.correct: Zn (134 pm) and Sn (151 pm) are close enough in size to Cu (128 pm) to take the places of Cu atoms in the lattice; neither is small enough to fit in the gaps.
options: Larger atoms cannot fit into the small gaps between metal atoms.
Only much smaller atoms, such as C, fit into the gaps; Zn and Sn are not much smaller than Cu.
Right: similar sizes, so they substitute.
An alloy is a mixture of a metal with another element, often another metal, as here.

items.q: Which claim about the data is best supported, with the right reasoning?
options: Brass is harder because Zn atoms are closer in size to Cu, so they bond more strongly
Bronze is harder because it contains more of the added metal than brass does
Bronze is harder because Sn differs more in size from Cu and disrupts the layers more
The three are about equally hard, since each wire still bends without breaking

why.correct: Bronze (95) is harder than brass (70), which is harder than pure Cu (50). Sn (151 pm) differs from Cu (128 pm) much more than Zn (134 pm) does, so each Sn atom distorts the layers more and makes sliding harder, even though bronze has far fewer added atoms (7% against 30%).
options: Brass (70) is softer than bronze (95), so the claim contradicts the data.
Bronze has fewer added atoms (7%) than brass (30%), yet is harder, so the amount alone cannot be the reason.
Right: the size mismatch, not the amount, fits the data.
Bending tells you they are still malleable; the hardness numbers range from 50 to 95.

items.q: Why can all three wires bend without breaking, unlike a crystal of an ionic solid?
options: As layers slide, the electron sea still surrounds each cation, so the bonding holds
The metals contain covalent bonds, which can bend without breaking
Metal atoms carry no charge, so they do not repel each other when the layers move
The wires are thin, and any thin solid bends rather than breaks

why.correct: In a metal the cations are held by delocalized electrons that move with them. When a layer slides, each cation is still surrounded by the electron sea, so the bonding is kept. In an ionic solid a shift brings like charges together and they repel.
options: Right: the electron sea follows the cations.
Copper and its alloys are held by metallic bonding, not covalent bonds.
Metals contain cations, which would repel each other if the electron sea were not between them.
A thin ionic crystal still snaps; thickness is not the reason.

items.q: All three wires conduct electricity well. Which feature of their structure explains this?
options: Pairs of electrons shared between two atoms
Cations and anions that are free to move about
Small atoms sitting in the gaps of the lattice
Delocalized electrons that can move through the solid

why.correct: Pure copper and both alloys are metallic solids. Their delocalized electrons are free to move, so they flow as a current when a voltage is applied.
options: Shared pairs are held between two atoms and cannot carry a current through the solid.
Metals contain cations but no anions, and their cations stay in place; it is the electrons that move.
None of these alloys has small atoms in the gaps (Zn and Sn substitute for Cu), and pure copper conducts too.
Right: mobile electrons carry the current.

items.q: Gold can be hammered into a sheet thin enough to see light through. Which explanation is best?
options: Gold is soft because its metallic bonds are much weaker than any other bonds
Its layers of atoms slide past each other while the electron sea holds them together
Gold atoms are very large, so there is a lot of empty space for them to move into
Each gold atom is bonded to just one neighbor, so the atoms are free to move about

why.correct: Malleability comes from layers sliding without breaking the metallic bond: the delocalized electrons surround the cations wherever they move.
options: Gold melts at over 1000 °C, so its bonding is not weak; it is malleable because its layers can slide.
Right: sliding layers held by the electron sea.
The cations are closely packed; it is sliding, not empty space, that lets the metal change shape.
Metallic bonding is not one bond between two atoms: each cation is attracted to the electron sea around it.

items.q: Steel for cutting tools is made by adding a small amount of carbon to iron. How does adding carbon change the iron?
options: It becomes softer and more malleable
It becomes harder and less malleable
It stops conducting electricity
It becomes brittle like an ionic solid, shattering when struck

why.correct: Carbon atoms are small, so they sit in the gaps between iron atoms (an interstitial alloy). They block the layers from sliding, which makes the steel harder and less malleable.
options: Blocking the layers makes sliding harder, not easier.
Right: the interstitial atoms pin the layers.
Steel is still metallic and still has delocalized electrons, so it conducts.
Steel is harder but still a metal; it bends before it breaks, unlike an ionic crystal.

items.q: A metallurgist adds a small amount of nitrogen (radius 71 pm) to pure iron (126 pm). Predict how each property changes.

variables.name: Hardness
variables.why: N atoms are much smaller than Fe, so they fit in the gaps and block the iron layers from sliding.

variables.name: Malleability
variables.why: With the layers pinned, the metal bends less easily before it breaks.

variables.name: Number of iron atoms in each layer of the lattice
variables.why: In an interstitial alloy the host atoms stay where they are; the small atoms go between them, not in place of them.

why.correct: Small atoms make an interstitial alloy: the lattice of the host metal is kept, but the extra atoms in the gaps resist sliding.

options: A metal whose atoms have been turned into anions by gaining electrons
A compound of a metal and a nonmetal with a fixed formula
A pure metal that has been melted down and then cooled again into a new shape
A mixture of a metal with other elements that keeps metallic properties

why.correct: An alloy is a mixture: its composition can vary (brass may be 60-80% copper), and it keeps metallic bonding and metallic properties.
options: Metals form cations, not anions; in an alloy the atoms keep sharing a sea of electrons.
An alloy is a mixture with a variable composition, not a compound with a fixed formula.
Melting and cooling a pure metal leaves it pure; an alloy has a second element.
Right: a metallic mixture.

items.q: Which properties can both pure metals and their alloys be expected to have? Select all that apply.
options: Good electrical conductivity
Good thermal conductivity
A single fixed formula
Brittleness

why.correct: Both are metallic solids with delocalized electrons, which carry electric current and also carry energy quickly through the solid.
options: Right: delocalized electrons carry charge.
Right: the mobile electrons also carry energy, so metals feel cold and heat up quickly.
Alloys are mixtures with variable composition, so they have no single fixed formula.
Metals and alloys are malleable; brittleness is typical of ionic solids.

items.q: Sterling silver is 92.5% silver (atomic radius 144 pm) and 7.5% copper (128 pm). Which classification and reasoning is best?
options: Substitutional: Cu atoms are close enough in size to Ag atoms to take their places
Interstitial: Cu atoms are smaller than Ag atoms, so they go into the gaps between them
Interstitial: there is much less copper than silver, so the copper fills the gaps
Substitutional: Cu and Ag are in the same group, so their alloys are substitutional

why.correct: Cu is about 11% smaller than Ag; atoms this close in size replace host atoms. Only much smaller atoms (such as C, N or B) fit in the gaps between metal atoms.
options: Right: the size match decides.
Being somewhat smaller is not enough to fit in the gaps between atoms; the gaps are far smaller than a Cu atom.
The amount of an element does not decide where its atoms go; their size does.
Group membership is not the reason; the similar atomic radii are.
